word:lxx:L712215.explanation: This verb means “break” or “crush,” describing an action that damages or separates something through force. As a verb, it presents breaking or crushing as an action rather than as an object, person, or place. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs twice: once in Jeremiah 27:23 and once in Ezekiel 29:7. These references show its use in two Old Testament passages, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular force or outcome in either passage.

word:lxx:L712259.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “fig yard,” referring to a place where fig trees are grown. It names the cultivated area rather than the fruit itself. The word occurs nine times across eight Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, including passages rendered with references to figs and a fig yard. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L712376.explanation: “Gathering” is the central meaning of this Greek LXX noun. It can describe people or things brought together, or the assembled group itself, according to the sentence. The word appears 218 times in the LXX corpus, including 200 occurrences in the Old Testament portion and 18 in the deuterocanonical books. Its repeated use across these writings shows a broad, ordinary sense centered on coming together as a group or collection. The precise force in any verse depends on what is being gathered and the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L712398.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to “relieve together” or “assist.” It describes helping share a burden so that another person is supported and the work becomes lighter. The idea is active cooperation rather than merely feeling concern from a distance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Exodus, Numbers, and Psalms. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains joining in help or relief.

word:lxx:L712400.explanation: This verb means to die with someone or to die together with others. It describes shared death, emphasizing that the persons involved undergo death together rather than separately. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Sirach 19:10. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself expresses dying alongside another person or group.

word:lxx:L712497.explanation: This noun refers to drawing something in or inhaling. Its central idea is an inward pulling or taking in, whether describing the act of drawing or the intake of breath. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 15:15. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of drawing in or inhaling.

word:lxx:L712509.explanation: Synteleia means consummation, a completion or ending.

word:lxx:L712545.explanation: This word means “wild swine; boar,” referring to a large, wild pig rather than a domesticated animal. It is a noun, so it names the creature itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 79:14. The approved English rendering there is “boar,” which confirms the ordinary animal sense. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: a wild pig or boar.

word:lxx:L712611.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “cord,” referring to a cord or line used as a tangible measure or boundary. In the Old Testament passages where it appears, the idea can be connected with portions of land or with something marked out and allotted, while still retaining its ordinary sense of a cord. It occurs 13 times in the Greek LXX, across 12 verses. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains a cord used materially or figuratively for an assigned measure.

word:lxx:L712628.explanation: This word is a proper name identifying Sōēa, also rendered Sia. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal or identifying name in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once, in Ezra 2:44, so its meaning is chiefly its identity rather than a broader concept developed through repeated use. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain whether it names a person, family, or group.

word:lxx:L712664.explanation: Sōphani, also rendered Sofani, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Numbers 26:43. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily its identification of a particular person or family connection in the biblical record, not a general concept used across many passages. The name itself does not provide enough information here to explain the person’s role or significance without the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L712884.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to courage—the boldness or resolve to undertake something difficult. It describes an inner readiness to act with confidence rather than shrink back. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, including two occurrences in Job and one in 2 Maccabees. Its central idea is daring initiative: a person possesses the courage needed to take on a challenging task or situation. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L713050.explanation: This verb means to treat someone with insolence—to insult or behave toward them in a disrespectful way. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it describes an action rather than a person or object. It occurs six times: four times in Old Testament verses and twice in Deuterocanonical verses. Its central idea is contempt expressed through conduct or words; the surrounding passage determines who is dishonored and how the insult is carried out.

word:lxx:L713102.explanation: Hyparchonta means belongings—goods or possessions that someone has.

word:lxx:L713256.explanation: Hypopherō means to bear up under.

word:lxx:L713506.explanation: This adjective describes someone who loves his own life and can therefore be characterized as cowardly. It points to a self-protective concern for preserving one’s life, rather than courage in facing danger or loss. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs only once, at Wisdom 11:26. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic meaning centers on strong attachment to life and the fearful conduct associated with it.

word:lxx:L713634.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “planting”—the act or result of putting a plant into the ground. It names planting as a thing rather than describing someone’s action. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in 2 Kings, Ezekiel, and Micah. Its occurrences are connected with the language of cultivated plants and their placement, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding text.

word:lxx:L713641.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “detect” or “discover”—to recognize or uncover something previously hidden, unnoticed, or unknown. It describes finding something out rather than merely possessing knowledge. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines what is detected or discovered in each use, but the central idea remains the uncovering or recognition of something.

word:lxx:L713678.explanation: Chaldaios refers to the Chaldeans, the people associated with the country of the Chaldees.

word:lxx:L713696.explanation: Chalou, also rendered Khalu, is a proper name for a place or person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual idea; it identifies a specific name. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Joshua 15:51. Because the available text does not provide the surrounding verse here, its precise referent is not further explained, but its lexical function is clear: it is a name rather than a common word with a broader everyday meaning.

word:lxx:L713713.explanation: Chananis, also written Khananis, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, identifying a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears three times in the Greek text of Numbers: Numbers 21:1, Numbers 21:3, and Numbers 33:40. These references establish where the name occurs, but the specific role or significance of the person must be understood from the verse and its surrounding passage. It is not a general term with a broader abstract meaning.

word:lxx:L713872.explanation: This word means “robe,” referring to a garment worn over the body. It is a noun naming a piece of clothing rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 12:35. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while the precise significance of the robe in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L713919.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “satisfy”: to provide what is needed so that a person, creature, or need is filled. It describes the result of receiving enough, whether the subject is nourishment or another provision. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, all within Old Testament books translated into Greek, with most occurrences in Psalms. The word’s precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains being supplied until the need is satisfied.

word:lxx:L713955.explanation: This verb means “prophesy”: to speak or declare a prophetic message. It describes the act of prophesying rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 45:4. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the action of delivering a prophecy.

word:lxx:L714099.explanation: This word means “water” or “liquid,” naming a physical substance. As a noun, it refers to water itself rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 12:15. Its basic meaning remains clear, while its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word’s single occurrence makes it a specific but straightforward term for water or another liquid substance.
